fomoOrdered.name: Document Crunch
fomoOrdered.fomoAngleOriginal: Other construction firms have already shifted contract review from 'read every document' to 'review the exception list.' Peerless is in the 'read every document' bucket right now. UC3 + UC4 move you to the exception list.
fomoOrdered.fomoAngleAdapted: The time Ashley spends reading every HS-105, 299A, 299B, and HS-118 by hand disappears on go-live day — construction firms that moved to exception-list review got that time back permanently. UC3 + UC4 build the same shift for Peerless's exact contract set.
fomoOrdered.savings: Contract review time reduced from weeks to minutes (vendor-reported)
fomoOrdered.aiAgentDescription: An AI agent reads every signed contract the moment it lands → extracts clause-level fields → validates them against the source quote and a rule library (price match, signature legibility, permit flag, deposit threshold) → flags only the exception cases for human review and routes them to the document owner before the job is opened.

challengeLead: 'It's never the same way' — Ashley's words about HD support — and 'We're considered legacy, so 4 hours, it won't be 2' from Brian about Deltek's SLA. These systems are archaic by design, not by accident. 'This is an ancient system. I feel like I've traveled back to the 90s.' That's the current state. The integration doesn't change ComputerEase or Home Depot Portal — it eliminates the human steps between them: the morning HD deposit check Ashley does by hand, the 1.5-hour ComputerEase rekey that follows every closed quote, and the document-by-document contract review. Those stop on go-live day.
closingLine: The Salesforce objects and MuleSoft event triggers established in Year 1 are what AgentForce reads in Year 2. That architecture is decided once.

talkingPoints.trigger: When they ask why MuleSoft instead of native Salesforce Flows or a simpler tool
talkingPoints.say: The hard part of this build isn't Salesforce — it's ComputerEase. The API doesn't live on the VM's external IP and it doesn't answer on port 443 or 8081. It runs through a Deltek-managed relay service called CE Live Service that's installed on the same VM, on port 445. Brian found this during our scoping sessions. Every architect who doesn't know that detail will either hit a wall or charge you to discover it. We found it in week one of scoping before we were engaged.
talkingPoints.impact: Prevents 2–4 weeks of dead-end debugging at the ComputerEase integration layer; CE Live Service relay identification is the single biggest risk-reduction milestone in the engagement

talkingPoints.trigger: When Ashley walks through her current morning routine or describes a typical day

Your Tuesday morning changes on day one of production.
talkingPoints.impact: 1.5h/job rekey eliminated across all closed quotes on go-live day; daily HD reconciliation pass eliminated; UC3+UC4 exception review replaces document-by-document review

talkingPoints.trigger: When Brian asks about the security posture of the integration or about the GCP firewall
talkingPoints.say: The integration doesn't touch your GCP VM's external IP at all. The ComputerEase connection goes to a Deltek-managed URL — that's the CE Live Service relay architecture you identified on April 17th. Once Jean's Deltek support ticket resolves and CE Live Service gets installed, the integration endpoint is Deltek's URL, not your firewall's problem. The MuleSoft tenant IP allowlist on the GCP ingress rule is the only firewall change needed, and you've already started that work.
talkingPoints.impact: GCP perimeter security preserved; CE Live Service relay keeps the integration off the customer VM's exposed external IP; no additional firewall exposure introduced

openingLines.line: Peerless is the Midwest anchor brand for Elevate Fence Partners' six-brand national platform — and the HD Portal to ComputerEase data path that every Home Depot Pro job runs through is the same template your five sibling brands will need when they scale. Brian has been in every scoping session making architecture decisions that are platform-standard, not Peerless-local. So we're scoping the Elevate template today, not just the Peerless instance. Ashley — walk me through what a Tuesday morning looks like, because every manual step you describe is something go-live day removes.

openingLines.context: If they say they already have a plan
openingLines.line: I'll take that and ask one question: does the plan account for the ComputerEase API not living on the GCP VM's external IP? The integration endpoint is a Deltek-managed relay URL routed through CE Live Service — not port 443, not the static IP Brian was debugging. If the plan routes to the VM directly, it'll work in a test environment and fail in production when CE Live Service isn't installed. That's the finding that changes the architecture, and we found it in week one of scoping before code was written.

Every week that doesn't start with UC2 in production is another week Ashley spends 1.5 hours per closed quote manually rekeying Salesforce data into ComputerEase — and the Elevate portfolio integration standard stays unset. Brian Cook has been in every scoping session making platform-architecture decisions. The window where Elevate's Director of IT is actively designing the template that will govern all 6 sibling company codes — and the architecture is still fluid — is the rarest deal-urgency condition we see. The template gets set once. It should be set intentionally.

openingLines.context: AI question — how does this help with AI?
openingLines.line: AgentForce works when there's a clean Salesforce object it can query — a Quote tied to a Lead tied to an HD F-number tied to a ComputerEase job number. Phase 1 builds exactly those joins. Without them, AgentForce can't answer 'which Wisconsin deposits missed 99%' or 'which jobs are trending over budget-worksheet target price before close-out' — Ashley has to open three systems manually to find those answers today. With Phase 1 complete, those questions become AgentForce queries. The Salesforce objects we define in Year 1 are what AgentForce reads. That architecture is decided once.

The hours-per-job figure lands before any technology mention.

costOfWaiting.basis: 1.5h per closed quote (sage.json Ashley Salerno manual rekey demo, 2026-04-16, confirmedFlows UC2) × conservative 5 HD jobs/week × 26 weeks = 195h in Salesforce→ComputerEase rekey alone. Weekly job volume not explicitly stated in scoping transcripts; 5 jobs/week is conservative for a 7-location regional fence contractor. Excludes daily HD reconciliation pass (~2.5h/week estimated from sage.json UC1 description) and contract document review (~2h/week from UC3 scope) — both separately documented manual activities.
costOfWaiting.sixMonthWindow: At a conservative 5 HD jobs per week, Peerless loses 195+ hours of Ashley's time over 6 months to manual ComputerEase rekey — before counting daily HD reconciliation or the document-by-document contract review. Every week after go-live recovers ~7.5 hours of operations capacity from UC2 alone. Waiting 6 months is 195 hours of manual labor that should have been automated. Confirm actual weekly job volume with Ashley to replace the conservative estimate with a client-specific figure.

A Salesforce-native Flows/Apex approach hits an architectural wall at the ComputerEase layer. DataSkate named this before the engagement started.
